You Wear It Well: Maruchan's Saucy Styles Reign as the Week's Best Work

Public Storage, Walmart, Banana Republic and CALPAK round out our Top 5

by David Gianatasio
October 29, 2026
10:45 am
2 min read
Share:

Here’s our roundup of the week’s Top 5, chosen by the Clios’ staff.

Bestie: It’s OK to Be a Hot Mess Sometimes, Maruchan Says

Maruchan feels you, Gen Z. And they made the cheeky wearables to prove it. Spent all your money at the bar? That’s what your T-shirt says. Ah well, at least you’ve got those Saucy Noods to savor. Developed with Goodby Silverstein & Partners and Beyond Studios’ creative director Cole Poska. Read More

2. Public Storage Tapped 4 Indie Filmmakers to Spin Terrifying Tales

What’s in those containers? Brand-boosting terror, that’s what! Microdrams are all the rage, and these vids from The Infinite Agency deliver a potent combination of thrills and chills for Spooky Season. Spoiler: That Teddy Bear ain’t right. See the trailer below. Read More and See All the Shorts Here

3. Walmart Reimagines ‘The Muppet Christmas Carol’ With Walton Goggins as Scrooge

Walton Goggins’ yuletide range is pretty impressive. After a winning turn as Walmart’s Grinch last year, he plays Ebenezer Scrooge in a musical, Muppet-y take on the holidays for 2026. Great spirit (heh) and production values from Fallon and director Randall Einhorn. Read More

4. Banana Republic’s Madcap Microseries Presents a Modern Travel Agency Living in the Analog Past

Jack Innanen handles 4 roles and brandishes a Crocodile Dundee-style bowie knife on the “adventure desk.” From the loopy travelers at COPE Global and Grand Nature, plus writer-director Jeffrey Scotti Schroeder. Read More

5. Marionettes Pull the Holiday Strings for CALPAK

OK, who wants to sit on Giant Puppet Santa’s lap? An oddly compelling early Xmas morsel from Bob Baker Marionette Theater, artist Jimmy Marble and digital creator Jillian Wheeler (who directed). Read More

entry.title: An Inside Look at Hoorae’s ‘Parental Advisory’ Reveals the Twists and Turns of Making Microdramas
entry.summary: Advertising An Inside Look at Hoorae's 'Parental Advisory' Reveals the Twists and Turns of Making Microdramas Muse visits the set to learn how brands and producers navigate the hottest trend in storytelling by T.L. Stanley October 28, 2026 1:45 pm 7 min read Share: The clock is t
entry.content:
Advertising

An Inside Look at Hoorae's 'Parental Advisory' Reveals the Twists and Turns of Making Microdramas

Muse visits the set to learn how brands and producers navigate the hottest trend in storytelling

by T.L. Stanley
October 28, 2026
1:45 pm
7 min read
Share:

The clock is ticking in the final hours of a seven-day shoot, and the summer sun is beating down on a rented Los Angeles bungalow that serves as a backdrop for the microdrama “Parental Advisory.”

Sometime after high noon, tragedy strikes, threatening to derail the project’s tight turnaround. One of the show’s stars is feeling dizzy and lightheaded from the triple-digit temperatures. Paramedics arrive as the cast and crew sweats, literally and figuratively.

“No one could’ve predicted a heat wave or a heat stroke,” said Dzifa Yador, head of digital at producer Hoorae. “And this impacts our no. 1 on the call sheet.”

After a health check on actor Grisselle Escotto, the decision comes down: She needs to stop filming, even though she has pivotal scenes and promotional vignettes with brand partner e.l.f. Cosmetics to complete.

Can this production be saved?

Pins and Needles

The cliffhanger is catnip—foundational, even—to the multibillion-dollar vertical series industry. In this case, the pins-and-needles development wasn’t scripted. It happened, though it took place behind the scenes rather than in the content itself.

A bit of life imitating art in a burgeoning genre that shrinks the classic TV soap opera into binge-worthy, bite-sized bits for a mobile audience. Relying heavily on exaggerated tropes and over-the-top twists, it gives viewers the dopamine hits that keep them coming back for more episodes. Think Pringles: once you pop, you can’t stop.

Skipping right to the spoiler: Escotto rallied and returned to set the next day, wrapping up the work right on schedule. Like the layered intrigue in “Parental Advisory,” everything resolves in the end.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by HOORAE, An Issa Rae Company (@hooraemedia)

Microdrama Machine

“Parental Advisory,” which dropped its 50-episode run on Oct. 28, comes from Issa Rae’s Hoorae as part of an ongoing deal with TikTok that brings exclusive series to the platform and its PineDrama app.

The relationship kicked off in April with “Screen Time,” a techno-thriller that instantly went viral, racking up 620 million global views and counting.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by HOORAE, An Issa Rae Company (@hooraemedia)

The second project, a 68-episode reality-dating show a la Temptation Island called “The Compatibility Experiment,” debuted Oct. 14, logging 110 million views so far.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by HOORAE, An Issa Rae Company (@hooraemedia)

And now there’s “Parental Advisory,” a whodunnit about bougie prep school families where it’s the grownups, not the kids, who’ve gone wild.

The three projects, in quick succession, are just the beginning. For 2027, Hoorae and TikTok plan to release a new microdrama every four to six weeks, each with brand financing and integration, according to Yador.

Muse got a peek into the making-of “Parental Advisory,” which churned out roughly an hour’s worth of entertainment with a fraction of the manpower, time and budget of a traditional Hollywood venture.

“We shoot 13-15 pages a day with one camera team, about 45 in the crew, seven in the cast—everything is as skeleton as it can be,” Yador said. “We have one or two takes to get what we need, and then we move on.”

Brand Backed, Not Brand Stacked

Even under those constraints, Hoorae Media and its sister company Ensemble are striving for premium-level storytelling.

“We’re making these series for audiences first,” said Ian Schaefer, Ensemble’s president and co-founder with Rae. “They’re not commissioned by brands. But we’re bringing brands in, integrating them in ways that feel natural.”

General Mills, with its Gushers candy, appeared in “Screen Time.” Alt soda Poppi and Sol de Janeiro perfumes cameoed in “The Compatibility Experiment.” e.l.f. has exclusivity in “Parental Advisory.” The brands enjoy active and passive placement, low-key enough not to trigger algorithms or get labeled “branded content.” The ad partners are disclosed.

“We don’t prioritize product over story—we do the opposite,” said Yador, noting that brand backing means the content is free for consumers to watch, where paywalls are common in the space. Brands that collaborate with Hoorae and Ensemble get an early look at the microdrama scripts and can share ideas. Their reps are invited to the set to oversee the brand’s face time. And they’re on hand IRL when the cast shoots themed vignettes that do “a lot of the heavy lifting” in cementing the sponsorship, Schaefer said.

A global ambassador from e.l.f. trained the stylist and makeup artist on “Parental Advisory,” and brand execs made sure Escotto’s character applied her bronzer and blush just-so during key scenes. (Brushes and strokes are everything).

Execs at e.l.f. were looking for “natural moments” in entertainment content instead of old-school product placement. “It’s all about being part of the storytelling, not interrupting it,” said Patrick O’Keefe, chief integrated marketing officer at e.l.f. Brands.

Microdramas were definitely on the radar for a brand that’s dabbled in mockumentaries, comedy shorts and other unconventional marketing meant to serve its loyalists and cultivate new customers.

“We’ve seen the power microdramas have with subcultures, and the impact Hoorae’s first series had was undeniable,” O’Keefe said. “When we looked at ‘Parental Advisory,’ we saw an organic way for e.l.f. to show up within a story our community would already be watching and talking about.”

Kitsch Is King

China may have birthed the microdrama, and remains the largest market globally for the snacky entertainment. But the U.S. has caught the bug. At its schlockier end, there are blockbusters like “My Gorgeous Wife Is an Ex-Convict,” “Never Divorce a Secret Billionaire Heiress” and the trend-right “Seducing My Hockey Rival.”

TechCrunch said the genre “feels like Cocomelon for adults,” and ad agency Walrus summed it up like this: “Think of the cheesiest thing you’ve ever seen on Lifetime and cut its budget by 80 percent—that’s a microdrama.”

Yet female millennials are passionate fans, part of an audience that spends more minutes a day with microdramas than with Netflix or Disney+, per Walrus. Short-drama apps like ReelShort, DramaBox and others reported 850 million downloads in Q1 2026, a 140 percent year-over-year leap.

TikTok recently signed its second microdrama deal with Made By Us Studios for creator-led vertical series, while legacy media has taken notice, with NBCUniversal, BET, A&E and Fox all announcing their entry into the space.

AI slop has arrived, not surprisingly, but Hoorae is committed to human talent with union memberships on all fronts. “We’re taking a more craft-driven approach,” Schaefer said, noting that Hoorae’s projects aim to break new talent and champion diverse voices.

Edge of the Seat

Appointment viewing, in the traditional sense, is a relic these days, replaced with what Schaefer calls “pass the time with” content. That’s where microdramas like “Parental Advisory” come in, offering high-concept 60-second episodes filled with lust, revenge, dark comedy and hyperbolic hijinks that make waiting in line at CVS a bit less painful.

The show, which brought back much of the crew from Hoorae’s previous vertical series, colors outside the lines in its true crime template (romance is the genre’s bread and butter). Producers study what’s fueling views, shares and convos across pop culture. Predictably, horror is on the future docket.

Back at the “Parental Advisory” set, director Kendall Outing runs through a scene with actor Raél Ba, searching for the right reaction when her character catches her straying husband on a mysterious phone call.

“Shimmy to the left, please, then give it a beat and cock your head,” Outing says, acting it out himself and advising against anything “too sitcom-y.”

Ba nails the “gotcha” moment, giving fellow actor Henderson Wade an appropriate jump scare.

Will this couple survive? Who else is cheating, in the bedroom and the boardroom, in this viperous social-climbing circle? And who gets bludgeoned at the fancy gala? The answers await here, one addictive minute at a time.

entry.content:
Advertising

It's OK to Be a Hot Mess Sometimes, Maruchan Says

Serving up merch that gets what you're going through

by Shahnaz Mahmud
October 28, 2026
1:00 pm
2 min read
Share:

In a bid to entice Gen Z, Maruchan’s Saucy Foods is acknowledging that being a hot mess is a part of its DNA.

The maker of instant Ramen and lunch noodles has partnered with Beyond Studios‘ creative director Cole Poska—known for his spins on branded merch—to devise a platform that includes clothing and a media campaign. Goodby Silverstein & Partners handled creative development.

The wearables include T-shirts and accessories that give fans permission to own their oft-messy lives. They sport lines like: “I spent all my money at the bar, at least I have Saucy Noods” and “I’m a hot mess with Saucy Noods.”

The impetus arose from fans creating their own Maruchan designs. 

“That inspired us to give fans a (brand-sanctioned!) merch line in collaboration with iconic designer Space Boy Cole,” says Charlotte Cordova, director of communication strategy at GS&P. “The campaign centers on how Saucy Noods are there for you in your hot-mess moments. We’re showing up with activations that position Saucy Noods as the go-to food for those moments: on social, in AI responses, in rideshare apps and now with a merch line.”

“We told Cole that everything we made for this line should support people in their moments of mess, so it made sense to include things like a Hot Mess hoodie, under-eye patches and a migraine mask,” adds creative director Kate Baynham. “Maruchan will be there for you no matter what.”

The merch is available for a limited time in Maruchan’s TikTok Shop.

The campaign can be seen on Snapchat ads that run after 9 p.m., via Uber ads that land after 7 p.m. and in partnership with TikTok show Are You Okay?, which celebrates people’s messy lives.

entry.content:
Advertising

Walmart Reimagines 'The Muppet Christmas Carol' With Walton Goggins as Scrooge

Following his epic turn as the Grinch from last year

by Christine Champagne
October 28, 2026
10:30 am
5 min read
Share:

Walton Goggins is back as the face of Walmart, this time stepping into the role of Ebezener Scrooge in a film inspired by The Muppet Christmas Carol. Riffing on that classic holiday flick, the spot finds Goggins surrounded by Kermit the Frog, Miss Piggy, The Great Gonzo, Rizzo the Rat and Pepé the King Prawn.

If you are a fan of Brooklyn Nine-Nine, you will get a kick out of seeing Stephanie Beatriz, beloved in the role of grumpy detective Rosa Diaz, as Scrooge’s cheerful niece. Kudos to the casting director for making this choice.

Directed by Randall Einhorn of Radical Media, the film launches Walmart’s broader “A Who Knew Carol” campaign. Through a series of videos and social content, the seasonal push finds the famously crotchety Scrooge discovering the plethora of gifts the retailer has to offer.

Here, Fallon CEO Nikki Baker discusses how Walmart’s association with Goggins—who suited up as the Grinch in a Walmart Black Friday campaign last year—benefits the brand. She also delves into the making of the hero film.

Why is Walton Goggins a great rep for the brand? And what was it like seeing him as Scrooge?

Walton brings so much energy and dedication to everything he does. He has become a true partner to our team over the last year and a half. He genuinely loves the work that we’ve been doing, and that passion comes through on the screen. Seeing him step into Scrooge was amazing because he brought depth and warmth to the role. He played Scrooge with real human emotion, which made his transformation and his rapport with the Muppets genuine and so much fun to watch.

The hero film is quite a production. Can you tell me about the thinking behind it as well as the campaign in general? 

The Muppet Christmas Carol is a masterclass in reappraisal—it’s all about taking a second look. At the end of the day, we wanted to build a fun holiday story that’s entertaining while also authentically bringing Walmart in. The musical numbers are a critical piece to what makes the original a fan favorite. We wanted to honor the fandom by kicking off the campaign with a musical number similar to the film. This Walmart-inspired number kicks off the season by launching “A Who Knew Carol” and establishing the universe, before we roll into a continuous campaign across the coming months that spotlights brand-name gifts, Black Friday savings and Express Delivery.

What was the biggest challenge in making the hero film?

Ensuring we were honoring the original Muppet classic while making sure the film delivered on Walmart’s business goals. The production was built on physical sets full of Easter eggs nodding to the original film and new music. Standing on set with Walton and the cast, seeing the incredible detail in every prop and costume, made all the magic.

Why was Randall Einhorn the right director to bring it to life? 

Randall has an incredible background in comedy and TV, so he knew exactly how to direct big performances and keep the story moving. He handled our hero broadcast and OLV films brilliantly. At the same time, our social video content was directed by SARBY, which is made up of Sara Cummings and Abby Gross, two of our creative directors at Fallon. They brought a fast, digital and culture-first perspective that made the social assets feel just as engaging as the musical film. 

I loved seeing the two old guys from the balcony as the ghosts.

We couldn’t do this without bringing back Statler and Waldorf, who played the Marley brothers in the original, and their signature heckling energy is perfect for our NFL spots. Across the whole campaign, every Muppet had a specific role to play. We brought in classic favorites, new Muppets and created our very own Muppet [a blue Walmart bag called Bagsy who appears in other videos but not the hero video], all with a goal to honor the original story while celebrating the holidays with Walmart.  

How did you incorporate gifts into the film and into the campaign in general? I love the teeny tiny lava lamp Pepé the King Prawn is holding.

Gifts can definitely sit in the background, but we prefer bringing them naturally into the story. We think it’s an incredible creative challenge, and we want to share the breadth of the gift assortment at Walmart. Whether it is a high-end De’Longhi espresso maker or a funny little detail like that tiny lava lamp, we wanted every product to feel like an authentic part of the scene.

This film is spirited and fun. Do you especially enjoy bringing big holiday stories like this to life? 

The secret to a lot of our work has been what we like to call “cultural commerce.” If people are entertained, they really do want to interact with your brand. It’s always great getting to build a story that people actually want to follow along with throughout the season. When you start with a great brand like Walmart and then bring together an amazing cast, real physical craft and iconic characters like The Muppets, it starts to feel like genuine entertainment. The campaign is festive, funny, and, hopefully, a fun break in the middle of a busy season.

entry.content:
Advertising

Public Storage Tapped 4 Indie Filmmakers to Spin Terrifying Tales

'Don't Watch' microdramas for Halloween. (That's just the title. They want you to watch)

by David Gianatasio
October 27, 2026
9:30 am
3 min read
Share:

So, people pack away unspeakable horrors in self-storage units these days. We’d suspected as much.

Such facilities serve as springboards for “Don’t Watch,” a quartet of unsettling micro-tales from Public Storage and The Infinite Agency. Unlike Yahoo’s somewhat similar Halloween offering, which spoofed Hollywood tropes for laughs, this frightful foursome plays it straight with the chills and suspense.

So, if you like skeletal remains, creepy mannequins, unlucky charms and breathless chases through dark woods that you know won’t end well … you’re kind of weird.

Which is awesome. Because this stuff’s for you.

Here’s a trailer that offers disturbing glimpses of what lies behind those roll-up doors:

Now, let’s look at the full tales, which run for a few minutes each. First, Emmy-winner Brandon Walker presents a collection of dusty, crusty remains that should have been left for dead:

@publicstorage 01_THE_COLLECTION.MP4 Content by: @watchfoundtv ♬ original sound – Public Storage

Next, writer-director Elaine Frost wonders if grandma will “still be there.” Unfortunately, in the end, we find out.

@publicstorage 02_FOREVER_YOUNG.MP4 Content by: @Deep Red Perfect Blue ♬ original sound – Public Storage

In our third installment, from Eric Orange, we learn why taking an unreliable 51-year-old truck on a cross-country trek during Spooky Season is a freakishly bad idea.

@publicstorage 03_MOVING_ON.MP4 Content by: @eric orange ♬ original sound – Public Storage

“We wanted to make something scary that didn’t feel like an ad. Public Storage were great partners,” Orange tells Muse. “They trusted us filmmakers to bring the thrills in an unexpected way. Love when brands listen to their audiences and aren’t afraid to take risks. If you’re going to be on social media as a brand, you should be having fun.”

Finally, our second ad this week with puppets in prominent roles. The first one featured merry Xmas marionettes. Jesse Blanchard’s “Teddy” poses a more sinister scenario:

@publicstorage 04_TEDDY.MP4 Content by: @Puppetcore ♬ original sound – Public Storage

“Storage can be a very mundane industry. That’s why we love when brands like Public Storage are unafraid to make it fun and show off a personality rarely seen from their peers,” says agency ECD Tim McCarthy. “So, with the uprising of the horror genre, and the increase in popularity of longer-form content on social like microdramas, we thought Halloween was the perfect time to play up the spooky misconception about the service they offer.”

Remember: “These videos are scary—but storing your stuff with Public Storage never is.” (But if you watch these and decide to just keep cramming mementos in the attic, who can blame you?)

Marionettes Pull the Holiday Strings for CALPAK

The luggage brand and Bob Baker Theater dial the whimsy up to 11

by David Gianatasio
October 26, 2026
1:00 pm
2 min read
Share:

Giant Puppet Santa’s not a Christmas tradition. What a shame. But CALPAK does its best to rectify this yuletide oversight in the minute-long spot below.

The luggage brand trades AI and other high-tech tricks for taut cords, steel rods and funny faces made from felt and fabric. Handcrafted figures from Bob Baker Marionette Theater anchor the holiday message.

There’s a mid-twentieth-century vibe at play. It’s like a commercial your grandparents might have seen on a local TV station back in the day.

Wags might suggest that Claus has been a corporate puppet for years, hell-bent on seasonal selling. We’d never stoop so low and risk coal in our stocking.

Kidding aside, it’s something different—a fresh take on familiar themes delivered in robust fashion.

“We wanted to partner with a fellow L.A.-centric institution, and Bob Baker has been creating memorable experiences for families for more than six decades,” says Jennifer Houston, CALPAK senior director of brand marketing. “That spirit of wonder and nostalgia felt like a natural fit for the story we wanted to tell. We chose to tell the story through the eyes of a child because kids have a way of finding magic in the little things adults sometimes rush past.”

The marionettes “gave the campaign a storybook quality we couldn’t have recreated from scratch,” she tells Muse. “Both brands also have an intergenerational appeal, which felt especially meaningful during a season centered on families coming together.”

Artist Jimmy Marble and digital creator Jillian Wheeler (who directed) helped bring the tale to life.

“One of the most exciting creative elements was the contrast between a classic holiday aesthetic and Los Angeles, a city better known for sunshine than snow,” Houston says. “That unexpected juxtaposition helped make the world of the campaign feel both familiar and new. The vintage car evokes the timeless feeling of a family road trip, while the marionettes bring a touch of handcrafted whimsy to the story.”

The campaign follows CALPAK’s unexpected teamup with Randy’s Donuts Last year for its Glazed Collection.

entry.title: Sarah Michelle Gellar Spoofs ‘Scream’ for Angry Orchard—and More Great Spooky Season Spots
entry.summary: Advertising Sarah Michelle Gellar Spoofs 'Scream' for Angry Orchard—and More Great Spooky Season Spots Our second helping of Halloween horrors, with Custom Ink, Hay Day and Bluebella's scary-sexy nightmare starring Sophia Hadjipantelli by Ads of the World October 26, 2026 9:00 am
entry.content:
Advertising

Sarah Michelle Gellar Spoofs 'Scream' for Angry Orchard—and More Great Spooky Season Spots

Our second helping of Halloween horrors, with Custom Ink, Hay Day and Bluebella's scary-sexy nightmare starring Sophia Hadjipantelli

by Ads of the World
October 26, 2026
9:00 am
3 min read
Share:

Here’s a selection of awesome All Hallows commercials, selected by Muse sibling Ads of the World.

Angry Orchard, ‘Mystery Caller’ featuring Sarah Michelle Gellar

Sarah Michelle Gellar, who met a grim end as Cici Cooper in Scream 2, plays herself as Ghostface rings again in a playful spot from Angry Orchard. The occasion: the cider maker’s Scream-themed Thriller Pack, with flavors like Headless Pumpkin and Mystery Caller. Let it go to voicemail, Sarah. Read More

Custom Ink, ‘Undead Acres’
Agency: Mekanism

What do monsters dress up as for Halloween? Us, apparently. Custom Ink’s AI-generated “Undead Acres” visits a crumbling suburb where zombies, vampires, witches and Frankenstein’s monsters cosplay as their favorite humans, decked out in personalized merch. Think wine-mom sippy-cup mugs and a Karen tracksuit demanding to speak to the manager. Turns out even the living dead want to express themselves. Spooky? Sure. Relatable? Frighteningly. Read More

Hay Day, ‘Haunted Farms’
Agency: Forsman & Bodenfors

Can ghosts play mobile games? Hay Day decided to find out. The cozy farming title sent Most Haunted’s Yvette Fielding to Cogges Manor Farm in Oxfordshire, reputedly one of Britain’s most haunted spots, to hold a séance. What she uncovered shaped the game’s new Halloween character, the Red Revenant. The film plays like a ghost-hunting doc, not an ad. Even the dead need to unwind. Read More

State Farm, ‘This Is a Halloween Nightmare!’
Agency: Highdive

In State Farm’s latest Halloween spot, a homeowner surveys a house crushed by a fallen tree and accidentally summons a cloaked creature of the night. Realizing it’s just property damage, the ghoul makes them sing the brand’s famous jingle instead, and a helpful agent shows up. Spooky? Barely. Neighborly? Definitely. Read More

Govee, Turn Up the Spooky

Sarah Michelle Gellar is having a busy Halloween. The Buffy star, who knows a thing or two about slaying, fronts Govee’s “Turn Up the Spooky. Slay Halloween.” The brand’s outdoor lights turn an ordinary house into a moody, cinematic haunt. Sarah’s pro tip: Spotlight one feature, like the roofline or a tree, and leave the rest in shadow. Less is more, even for vampire slayers. Read More

Bluebella, ‘No Place Like Home’
Agency: Riff Raff Films

There’s no place like home, unless home turns into a horror movie. Lingerie brand Bluebella gets dark and surreal for Halloween with a fever-dream starring Sophia Hadjipantelli, whose familiar surroundings morph into a shadowy, seductive hellscape. Borrowing from classic terror trailers, it flips the genre’s habit of punishing confident women, casting her as the one in control. She’s not a scream queen—she’s more like a scream boss. Read More

entry.summary: Advertising Banana Republic's Madcap Microseries Presents a Modern Travel Agency Living in the Analog Past Jack Innanen plays 4 roles—and he carries a knife. Nothing strange there by David Gianatasio October 22, 2026 10:00 am 4 min read Share: Gap Inc.’s Banana Republic takes a t
entry.content:
Advertising

Banana Republic's Madcap Microseries Presents a Modern Travel Agency Living in the Analog Past

Jack Innanen plays 4 roles—and he carries a knife. Nothing strange there

by David Gianatasio
October 22, 2026
10:00 am
4 min read
Share:

Gap Inc.’s Banana Republic takes a trip back in time with a micro-mockumentary series chronicling a travel agency where staffers rely on analog tech to get the job done.

Is it faxtastic? Let’s just say an amusing improv vibe drives the first two installments, stoking nostalgia that should resonate with a range of viewers—especially those who inhabited the Clinton years (or wish they had).

Jack Innanen (from Adults) shines in multiple roles, including the every-bro office manager, a lothario who sells cruise packages and the “adventure desk” guy brandishing a Crocodile Dundee-style hunting knife.

When a corporate drone (Taylor Ortega) arrives to modernize “The Agency,” everyone’s thrown into a tailspin. The second of five episodes, each running about 2 minutes, dropped today across social:

COPE Global and production studio Grand Nature developed the project. (They previously partnered on “The Scene,” a Marc Jacobs microseries starring Rachel Sennott. Writer/director Jeffrey Scotti Schroder and veteran cinematographer Sean Price Williams (famed for his handheld camera style) also contributed.

The team developed several ideas as a springboard based on Banana Republic’s desire to focus on “adventure.” One of these “was ‘The Last Travel Agency in NYC,'” Grand Nature CCO and executive producer Brianna Sedor tells Muse. “Travel agencies, to us, felt like a funny take on the concept of adventure. And the idea of analog being forced to modernize felt like a particularly relevant storyline given where we’re at in the world today.”

Of course, short brand series are having a moment, so “The Agency” represents a chance for the retailer to flex across a trending format.

“Across the board, audiences are viewing content and advertisements in less traditional ways, but especially younger people,” Sedor says. “They want more from their targeted content—which they should! Banana Republic was looking for a fresh approach to share the brand with the social-first generation in a way that resonates. This micro-series does just that.”

“The work we put into the writing of this was in service to those watching it and I think it shows. Putting TV-level writing into targeted content is so worth it. We want this to be enjoyable for everyone.”

But, why cast Innanen in multiple roles?

“Jack’s original claim to fame is on TikTok having conversations with himself as different characters,” she says. “He already plays multiple roles in his videos, and we wanted to capitalize on what he does best. Also, he is just the most charming and kindest person ever. He is amazing in Adults and Big Mistakes, so hiring him as an actor was a no brainer. It was a huge bonus when we realized he can play mockumentary as good as anyone on The Office.”

What’s more, a BTS element will come into play, with real crew members—Sedor included—appearing on camera.

“Everyone played heightened, or let’s call it satirical, versions of themselves,” she says. “It adds a lot of great assets for people to watch. Even though they’ve finished the series, there’s more content surrounding the show that they can keep binging. And even better, this is real BTS, which you don’t get that often with ads or content in general.”

entry.title: Cerveza Victoria Created a Touching Tribute, With Hummingbirds, for Mexico’s Day of the Dead
entry.summary: Advertising Cerveza Victoria Created a Touching Tribute, With Hummingbirds, for Mexico's Day of the Dead Stop-motion and live-action techniques honor heartfelt traditions by Shahnaz Mahmud October 21, 2026 11:30 am 3 min read Share: To commemorate Mexico’s Day of the Dead , Cerve
entry.content:
Advertising

Cerveza Victoria Created a Touching Tribute, With Hummingbirds, for Mexico's Day of the Dead

Stop-motion and live-action techniques honor heartfelt traditions

by Shahnaz Mahmud
October 21, 2026
11:30 am
3 min read
Share:

To commemorate Mexico’s Day of the Dead, Cerveza Victoria wished to capture the traditional belief that loved ones who have passed take the form of hummingbirds to visit those they’ve left behind. So, the maker of the first Mexican lager beer created “Love is Eternal.” It features 2,352 frames, 4,013 handmade flowers and Juan Gabriel—considered Mexico’s Elton John—for a tale mixing live-action footage with stop-motion imagery.

Wieden+Kennedy Mexico developed the campaign. It was directed by The Youth, the Brazilian trio consisting of Eduardo Lubiazi, João Machado, and Yuri Maranhão, with YUCA overseeing the stop-motion and animation process.

The film takes viewers through one man’s remembrance of his beloved wife while frequently cutting away to a hummingbird in flight. It also shows others mourning the loss of their loved ones as they prepare for the Día de Muertos. 

The goal is to remind people that love doesn’t end when someone is gone, even if it feels that way.

“As long as we keep remembering those we’ve lost, their love remains eternal,” says the agency’s CCO Jessica Apellaniz. “What makes this belief so special is that it goes far beyond Día de Muertos. On any given day, at any unexpected moment, a hummingbird might appear, bringing with it the feeling that someone you love has come back to see you. That simple but powerful idea became one of the biggest inspirations behind our creative process.” 

The decision to make a hybrid film was based on the emotionality of the story, which required a human touch. 

The goal was the create a defined contrast between “Mictlán,” the afterlife where the souls of loved ones come from, and the real world. The hummingbird itself was hand-carved from wood.

“One allowed us to explore magical realism, creating a dreamlike world filled with cempasúchil flowers as the hummingbird made its journey, the other grounded the story in the everyday reality of Mexico, until, finally, both worlds came together in a long-awaited reunion,” says Apellaniz. “Together, all these elements helped us create something that people are not only talking about and sharing, but also connecting with on a deeper level, reminding us how special it is to be Mexican and to have traditions like these.”

The work uses “Amor Eterno” sung by Gabriel, who passed away 10 years ago. The song has become an anthem of Day of the Dead across the country.

“Every time you hear it, you can’t help but think of the loved ones you miss,” says W+K creative director Javier Melo. “And for a story this ambitious, we needed a soundtrack that could live up to that emotion and bring warmth to people’s hearts,” adds Kevin Murcia, also a CD at the agency.

The film took four months to make, requiring over 125 hours of stop-motion work. The film is nearing 50 million views in 10 days and will run through Dec. 6 in various media.

“We also want to dedicate this film to Rodrigo del Oso, one of the creative directors who helped shape Victoria into the brand it is today and who sadly passed away a few years ago,” says Apellaniz. “His photograph appears in the film as a small tribute to him and everything he contributed to the brand.”
